This sector includes emerging sectors such as hydrogen exports, aviation, off-road equipment, specialty chemicals, and others. While not providing concrete hydrogen demand projections for LH - 2 powered aircraft, the hydrogen roadmap does provide insights as to the threshold price LH must 2 be dispensed into aircraft (i.e., the price the aircraft owner pays). The hydrogen threshold price for aviation may be in the range of $4/kg–$5/kg, similar to the medium- and heavy-duty vehicles price range, because jet fuel has both a similar price and gravimetric energy density as gasoline and diesel used for vehicles. The exact price threshold where hydrogen becomes competitive with jet fuel will ultimately depend on factors including, but not limited to, price of jet fuel, the efficiency of a hydrogen-powered propulsion system compared to the incumbent jet engine propulsion system, and any payload capacity losses due to the lower volumetric energy of LH 2 compared to jet fuel. High jet fuel prices, high hydrogen propulsion system efficiency, and no payload capacity reduction with hydrogen-powered aviation (compared to similarly sized and designed conventional aircraft) would be the ideal conditions for hydrogen demand for aviation to scale. This scenario would lead to a high hydrogen threshold price. For reference, the price of hydrogen at light-duty refueling stations in California reached more than $30/kg in 2024. However, this high price was primarily driven by hydrogen supply disruptions that left stations without fuel. Retail hydrogen prices in Europe, South Korea, and Japan were in the range of $7–$16/kg in 2024 (Collins 2024). With the learning taken from these first-of-their-kind refueling stations in California, and as the hydrogen supply chain in the United States matures, hydrogen retail prices at the pump would be expected to drop, especially for new end-use applications like heavy-duty trucking and eventually LH -powered aviation. 2 In 2024, NLR published a report titled Levelized Cost of Dispensed Hydrogen for Heavy-Duty Vehicles, which indicated that the cost of gaseous hydrogen dispensed into heavy-duty trucks and delivered via liquid hydrogen tanker trucks could range between $6.50/kg and $11.20/kg around 2030 depending on the refueling demand and station utilization rate (Figure 45) (Bracci et al. 2024). While these costs are specific to heavy-duty vehicle hydrogen demand, the only significant infrastructure change for aircraft hydrogen demand is in the refueling station because the hydrogen would be a cryogenic liquid instead of gaseous when dispensed into aircraft. When dispensing LH , the requirement for high-cost compressors is eliminated, and total refueling 2 station cost may be comparatively lower (Elgowainy 2024). However, by the next decade it is likely that hydrogen demand for aircraft at airports will be on the order of 1 MTPD or less, meaning the higher-cost values under the “2 MTPD” section of Figure 45 would be most relevant.
